title: Financial thinking
subtitle: Knowledge is not the missing part - how you think is
openingQuestion: Is the home you live in an asset or a liability?
openingOptions: An asset, because property in general tends to appreciate over the long run
It depends on the cash flow: a home you live in takes money out every month
A liability, because every loan is a liability
An asset, because it sits on your personal balance sheet
explanation: The test is not the label but the direction of the cash flow: what puts money in your pocket is an asset, what takes money out is a liability. The same house falls into either group depending on how it is used - a rented-out house collects money every month, while the one you live in costs mortgage interest, tax, management fees and repairs. That does not make buying a home to live in wrong: it meets a real need, and not every decision should be optimised for cash flow. It only means you should not count the home you live in among the things currently feeding you when you tally up what actually produces income.

diagram.label: Buy things that produce cash flow
That cash flow pays for your spending

realWorldExample.description: Two people both earn 20 million and both reach 30 million after five years. The one who held their standard of living steady and pushed the whole raise into investments ends those five years with capital already earning for them; the one whose spending rose with their salary keeps the same savings rate - a higher income, but no closer to financial independence.

sections.text: Most personal finance knowledge is neither difficult nor secret. What separates two people on the same income is a handful of habits repeated long enough, plus one simple test applied to every large purchase.
Assets and liabilities: the test is cash flow

left.label: Puts money in your pocket
left.text: Shares and ETFs, rental property, a stake in a business that generates cash, savings that earn interest.

right.label: Takes money out of your pocket
right.text: A car bought on instalments for getting around, a high-rate credit card balance, luxury goods on deferred payment - and the home you live in while the mortgage is still running.

sections.label: Do not turn this into a hard rule
sections.text: The same house can sit in both columns depending on how it is used, so this is a test for seeing clearly, not an instruction to sell up and rent. Buying a home to live in meets a real need; just do not count it among the things currently feeding you.
Time does most of the work

items: Start at 25, contribute 5 million a month at 10% a year: roughly 4.5bn by 65
Start at 35, same contribution and same rate: roughly 1.7bn
Those first ten years change the outcome by nearly threefold, while the total contributed differs by only about three tenths

sections.text: That is why the question worth asking is not how much to contribute each month but when to start. Adding two million a month does not make up for ten years already gone, because most of the final figure comes from interest earning interest rather than from the principal.
The order of the four layers

items: An emergency fund of 3-6 months of spending, so one incident does not force you to sell assets early or borrow at a high rate
Clear high-rate debt, credit card balances and consumer loans first
Save at least 20% of income - the 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% saving and investing frame
Track your personal cash flow: knowing where the money goes is the precondition for controlling it
Study finance 15 minutes a day - knowledge compounds over time too

lines: Move the savings out the moment your salary lands, before you spend, rather than saving whatever is left - because usually nothing is.
And when your pay rises, hold your standard of living steady for a while: that is the cheapest moment to lift your savings rate.

quiz.question: According to Rich Dad Poor Dad, what is the main difference between the rich and the poor?
options: The rich buy assets, the poor buy liabilities
The rich work harder, so they earn more
The rich manage to save more because they spend less
The rich have more education
quiz.explanation: Kiyosaki: an asset is something that puts money in your pocket (shares, rental property, a business). A liability is something that takes money out (a consumer car, a home you live in). The rich accumulate assets.

quiz.question: When does compound interest work best?
options: The higher the rate the better; time matters less
Over the longest possible investment horizon
With the largest possible principal
With interest credited as often as possible
quiz.explanation: Time is the strongest factor in compounding because its effect is exponential. 100 million at 10% a year for 30 years reaches 1.7bn. Over 40 years, 4.5bn.

quiz.question: What does 'pay yourself first' mean?
options: Paying yourself a salary before your staff
Buying things for yourself before paying the bills
Moving savings out before you start spending
Giving yourself a raise whenever the company does well
quiz.explanation: Pay yourself first: the moment your salary arrives, move X% into the investment account before spending. Do not wait to 'save what is left' - usually nothing is.

quiz.question: What is lifestyle inflation and why is it dangerous?
options: Inflation making an individual's cost of living more expensive
Living costs rising with age
A pay rise arriving alongside rising prices
Spending rising by exactly as much as income rises
quiz.explanation: Lifestyle inflation: pay rises 20% and spending rises 20% too, so the savings rate does not move. Wealthy people hold their lifestyle steady as income rises and invest the difference.

quiz.question: Under sound financial thinking, what should come first?
options: Building an emergency fund of 3-6 months of spending
Buying a home - property is the best investment there is
Investing in shares, to start compounding early
Clearing all debt before thinking about investing
quiz.explanation: The emergency fund is the mandatory foundation. Without it, any incident - job loss, illness - forces you to sell investments early or borrow at a high rate.

keyTakeaways: The asset-or-liability test is the direction of the cash flow, not the name of the thing
Time is the strongest variable in compounding - starting ten years earlier beats contributing more each month
Move the savings out the moment you are paid; do not save what is left over
If spending rises with every pay rise, the savings rate stands still

summary.keyIdea: Wealth is not measured by income but by the share of income turned into things that produce money themselves
summary.commonMistake: Letting spending rise by exactly the size of the pay rise, and mistaking that for getting ahead
summary.action: Set up an automatic transfer into the investment account on the day your salary lands

application.title: Do this month
application.message: Take the last three months of statements, sort every outgoing into things that put money in your pocket and things that take money out, then work out what percentage of your income goes towards the first group each month.
application.secondary: If the figure is below 20%, the fix is usually not in your income but in your second and third largest expenses.

practicePrompt.question: Your salary rises from 20 to 25 million. You were saving 4 million a month, which was 20%. To hold your standard of living steady, what should you do?
options: Save 9 million: keep spending at the same 16 million as before
Save 5 million, to keep the same 20% rate as before
Save 4 million as before, and use the increase to live a little better
Wait until year end to see actual spending before deciding
practicePrompt.explanation: Holding your standard of living steady means holding the amount spent steady, not the rate. The old spending was 20 - 4 = 16 million, so after the raise savings become 25 - 16 = 9 million and the rate jumps to 36%. Keeping the 20% rate is the tempting mistake: it lets spending rise to 20 million, so four fifths of the raise is absorbed by lifestyle.
